study.title: Judges 13 - The birth of Samson and the beginning of liberation
study.overview: Judges 13 opens Samson's account by showing, first, the spiritual fall of Israel and its oppression by the Philistines forty years; then God's sovereign initiative in announcing the birth of a deliverer through a barren woman. The chapter highlights that salvation begins even before the child is born: God calls the mother to a special consecration, reveals himself tremendously to the couple and, finally, causes the Spirit of the LORD to begin to act in Samson. The text does not yet present the victories of the judge, but prepares everything for divine grace, by promise and separation for the service of God.

outline.title: Israel in sin, oppression, and promise of a son
outline.explanation: The chapter begins with the pattern already known in Judges: Israel does evil, and the LORD gives it over to the Philistines forty years. In this scenario of discipline, Manoah's Zorah, of the tribe of Dan, and his wife, barren, arises. The angel of the LORD announces that she will conceive of a son, who is to be separated from the womb from the womb as a Nazirite, and that this child will begin the salvation of Israel from the hand of the Philistines.

outline.title: Confirmation of the message and the instructions for consecration
outline.explanation: The woman relates the appearance to her husband with reverence and precision, not knowing the name of the messenger. Manoá prays asking for a new visit and instruction on the boy. God answers, and the angel repeats the directions: the mother must keep himself separated from wine, strong drink and unclean food. The focus is not curiosity, but obedience: the child belongs to God since before birth.

outline.title: The sacrifice, revelation, and the beginning of the Spirit's action
outline.explanation: Manoah tries to honor the visitor with food, but the angel guides him, if there is burnt offering, to be offered to the Lord. When the sacrifice is presented, the angel rises in the flame, performing something supernatural before the couple, who then recognizes his identity. Manoah fears dying of seeing God, but his wife interprets the facts with hope. The chapter ends with the birth of Samson, the blessing of the LORD upon him and the beginning of the manifestation of the Spirit of the LORD in his life, between Zorah and Staol.

study.context: The text situates history in the period of judges, when the people live a recurring cycle of sin, discipline and help. Here Israel suffers under the hand of the Philistines, and the promised deliverer comes from a common family of Dan in Zorah. The notes also note that Samson is presented as the last judge whose story is recorded in this book, and that his ministry begins unusually, before any public office or military campaign.
study.theology: The chapter emphasizes God's gracious initiative. Liberation is not born of the merit of Israel, but of divine fidelity in the midst of the unfaithfulness of the people. The sterility of the woman makes the promise even more evident: the child will be a gift of God, not a result of human capacity. The consecration Nazirrhea shows that the liberator belongs to the LORD in a special way and is separated for a mission. The truth also appears that God acts by veiled means: the angel of the LORD is recognized only after the fact, and revelation provokes fear, worship, and discernment. Finally, the Spirit of the LORD is the source of the beginning of Samson's work; the liberation of Israel depends not only on human force, but on the action of God that awakens and sustains his servant.

scholarViews.insight: The birth of Samson confirms God's faithfulness to his promise: a stellar woman gives birth, showing that no word of the LORD fails.
The Spirit of the LORD begins to move Samson, producing in him a strong desire to act for the liberation of the people, and this occurs still in the family environment between Zorah and Staol.

questions: What does the beginning of the chapter teach about how God acts when his people are spiritually in decline?
Why is the consecration of the mother and the child so important to understand Samson's mission?
How does the reaction of Manoah and his wife help to perceive the difference between fear, faith and discernment before the presence of God?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to recognize that restoration begins with repentance and dependence on God, not with self-confidence. It also invites to value consecration in daily life: to separate from what contaminates, obeying the Lord's instructions and to hope that the work of liberation will come from the Spirit of God, not only from natural talents. In practice, it is worth examining which areas of life need greater submission to God so that their mission is not obscured by personal impulses.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text provided and the notes are partially summarized; therefore, some historical and interpretative observations were kept only at the level explicitly supported by the material given. The notes of Matthew Henry and Adam Clarke appear truncated at certain points, so the above summaries reflect only what was provided. No external data on dates, broad geography, archaeology or original terms have been added.
